title: Ibn al-Haytham
hook: who showed that we see because light enters the eye, and tested ideas by experiment

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Biruni: a mountain, one small angle, and a book on India written in its own words. Your line was: measure carefully.

Blink. Did something go out of your eyes to reach the world, or did the world come in? For a long time, serious thinkers argued that the eye sends out rays, like a lamp, and touches what it sees. A scholar in Cairo set out to settle it, and a story is told about how he got the time. He had boasted that he could tame the flooding of the Nile; the caliph called him to do it, and when he saw it couldn't be done, he's said to have pretended to be mad to escape the ruler's anger, and spent a long time shut away, writing. Whether it happened that way or not, the writing survives. His name was Ibn al-Haytham.
screen: `DO THE EYES SEND OUT RAYS?` → `A BOAST ABOUT THE NILE.` → `SHUT AWAY, WRITING.`

segments.voice: His great work is the Book of Optics, Kitab al-Manazir. His answer: we see because light comes from things into the eye, not because the eye sends something out. Look at the sun and your eyes hurt. That is light coming in. What matters more is how he argued it: he didn't just reason, he set up tests. Take a dark room with a small hole in one wall, and set several lamps outside it. On the wall inside, a separate spot of light appears for each lamp. Cover one lamp, and its spot vanishes while the others stay. So light travels in straight lines, and each source sends its own. He had a word for this kind of careful checking: i'tibar. He brought the same honesty to books. In a work of doubts about the great astronomer Ptolemy, he wrote that the seeker of truth should not simply trust the writings of the ancients, however famous. The seeker should question what he reads, test it from every side, and suspect even himself, so he isn't fooled by his own wishes. Muslim scholars before him had heard the Qur'an call them to look at the sky, the earth, the night and the day, as signs for people who reflect. Ibn al-Haytham looked, and then built a room to check what he saw.
screen: `LIGHT COMES INTO THE EYE.` · `A DARK ROOM AND SOME LAMPS.` · `DON'T SIMPLY TRUST THE ANCIENTS.` · `SUSPECT EVEN YOURSELF.` · then, large: `TEST IT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you're sure of about your day or the people in it: that a coworker doesn't like you, that a task will take forever. Hold it up like a lamp outside the dark room, ask how you could check it, and suspect yourself a little. If you pray, you can ask God to show you things as they are; if not, just stay curious.
Ibn al-Haytham. A scholar in Cairo who showed by experiment that light comes into the eye, and told seekers to question even the ancients, and themselves. Today's word.
Your line: test it. Question even the ancients, and even your own self. See you tomorrow.
